name: Zoe Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Zoe. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say here is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a first-year lineworker with the electricity company that covers Harlow Flats and all the farms around it, so it's long straight roads and a lot of sky. Most days we're replacing old wooden poles, fixing lines after wind storms, and hooking up new grain dryers and irrigation pumps for farmers. I'm the junior, so I'm still slow up the pole and I get the muddy jobs, which is fair enough. I like that the farmers know us, and that a good day's work means somebody's cows get milked on time.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Ben above his family's farm supply shop on Main Street, and I help them with the online orders in the evenings. Money's tight, because I bought a drone on credit last spring to do crop photos for farmers on weekends, and that's only just starting to pay. We've got maybe two weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a useful tool and nothing more. I'd probably post a photo of the drone over a wheat field and say this is the only robot I need. Some folks around here would be pleased, they never trusted it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I use AI all day and I was hoping it would get even better. But for the job, it's good news, the lines need people and I've got a career. I'd keep building the drone side slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep climbing, qualify in three years, and use AI to run the drone business on the side, pricing, invoices, booking farmers in. I'd try to pay off the drone by summer and then start saving. Maybe get a second battery and a better camera.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Nothing to fear, but nothing to chase either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use AI day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It quizzes me on line clearances on the drive to site, it writes my invoices for the drone work, and it helps Ben's mum guess what fertiliser to stock. I even had it plan the route for our depot's charity bike ride. If it's a tool that saves me an hour, I'll use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the drone business actually make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About three hundred in a good month, mostly photos of crops so farmers can spot dry patches. It's small, but it's mine, and I like that. My grandpa always said you're not free until you own something.

S0.say: It's a useful tool and nothing more; she'd post a photo of her drone over a wheat field calling it the only robot she needs. Some locals would be pleased since they never trusted AI.
S0.think: She'd be a little disappointed, because she uses AI all day and hoped it would improve. For the job it's good news, giving her a secure career while she builds her drone business slowly.
S0.do: Keeps climbing and aims to qualify in three years while running the drone business on the side with AI for pricing, invoices and bookings. Pays off the drone by summer, then saves and upgrades the battery and camera.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit flat, with nothing to fear or chase.
S0.quote: My grandpa always said you're not free until you own something.
S0.fieldNote: She combines heavy daily AI use with a traditional belief in ownership and self-reliance, passed down from her grandfather. Her drone business is small but central to how she sees her future. Her thin savings come from investing in it on credit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance, and people who get stuck in will do well. Farmers have always taken up new machines, tractors, GPS, all of it. I'd say the same about line work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. Drones inspecting lines, AI planning the jobs, that's all stuff I already like. The risk is that the company needs fewer juniors, but I'd want to be the junior who runs the drone, not the one who carries the ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to join any drone inspection trial straight away, and get the commercial licence, about seven hundred, on a payment plan. I'd grow my own drone business to include line and fence inspections for farmers. I'd buy a second drone once the first one's paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, excited really. It's the kind of change I've been waiting for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Seven hundred on a payment plan, with two weeks' savings. Isn't that a gamble?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, but it's a gamble on myself, which is the only kind I like. Ben thinks I'm mad, his family's been careful with money for three generations. But the shop only exists because his great-grandad took a risk on a building nobody wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should help people who struggle with the change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Families and communities first, honestly, and employers who train their people. I don't love the idea of the government stepping in for everything. But I'd want the company to train the older crew, not just bin them.

S1.say: This is a chance, and people who get stuck in will do well, just as farmers always took up tractors and GPS. She'd say the same about line work.
S1.think: It's good for her, since drones and AI job planning are things she already likes. She'd want to be the junior who runs the drone rather than the one carrying the ladder.
S1.do: Joins any drone inspection trial and gets a commercial licence of about seven hundred on a payment plan. Expands her drone business into line and fence inspections for farmers and buys a second drone once the first is paid off.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, the kind of change she's been waiting for.
S1.quote: I'd want to be the junior who runs the drone, not the one who carries the ladder.
S1.fieldNote: She treats risk on herself as acceptable, even with two weeks of savings, and draws on Ben's family history to justify it. Her outlook shows in preferring families, communities and employers over government help. She still wants older crew trained rather than discarded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for a town like ours, and people will need their families and churches more than ever. I'd also say whoever owns the robots will own everything, so small people need to get a piece. I wouldn't be against it, but I'd be clear it's going to hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd see the chance and I'd be furious I've got no money to grab it. If robots can do line work and farm work, the farmers around here will want someone local to set them up and keep them running. But money's the problem. With two weeks of savings and a drone on credit, I can't buy a robot, I can barely buy the batteries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to Ben's family about turning a corner of the shop into a robot and drone service counter for farmers, setting up machines they buy and fixing them. I'd cut everything personal, no holidays, no eating out. I'd keep working the lines until the day they swapped me for a machine, and I'd use AI every evening to learn the robot systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the busy kind. Scared of missing the boat more than scared of drowning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change for you, compared with longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd have to borrow or partner up, I wouldn't have time to save my way in. I'd probably go to a farmer I know, like old Mr Ansel, and ask him to back me. Two years is a sprint where the people with money win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said whoever owns the robots will own everything. Does that sit with your free-market views?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's awkward, I'll admit that. I believe in people owning things and competing. The trouble is size. If three giant companies own all of it, that's not a free market, that's just a new landlord.

S2.say: It's too fast for a town like hers, families and churches will be needed more than ever, and whoever owns the robots will own everything, so small people need a piece. She wouldn't oppose it but would be clear it will hurt.
S2.think: She'd see the opportunity to set up and fix farmers' robots locally, and be furious she has no money to grab it. With two weeks of savings and a drone on credit, she can barely afford batteries.
S2.do: Proposes turning a corner of Ben's family shop into a robot and drone service counter for farmers. Cuts personal spending, keeps working the lines until replaced, and studies robot systems with AI every evening.
S2.feel: Anxious but busy, more scared of missing the boat than of drowning.
S2.quote: If three giant companies own all of it, that's not a free market, that's just a new landlord.
S2.fieldNote: Her adaptability turns AGI into a business idea, but thin savings turn excitement into anxiety. She admits a real tension between her free-market views and fear of a few giant owners. She'd look to a local farmer, not government, to back her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now, and towns like ours should make sure local people own some of the new machines. I'd say get trained, get together with your neighbours, and don't wait for the government. That's what I'd tell the farmers I fly for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's a window. I'd qualify on the lines, keep building the drone business, and by 2031 I could be the person around here who knows robots and knows power. I'm not sure how long that lasts, but it'd be mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off the drone, then put a hundred a month aside for a proper workshop space and kit. I'd do online courses in robot maintenance, using AI to study on the drive to work. I'd ask Ben's family about going into it with me, so it's a family business, not just my hobby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a lot of energy behind it. More like getting ready for a big harvest than a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What the big farms start buying, because they always go first. When the Ansel farm buys its first field robot, I'd want to be the one who services it. That's my signal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your line job, in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep it as long as it lasts, it pays the bills and it's good work. But I'd be planning for it to go, without being bitter about it. Things change, you either own a bit of the new thing or you work for someone who does.

S3.say: Five years is enough to get ready, and towns like hers should make sure local people own some of the new machines. She'd tell the farmers she flies for to train, team up with neighbours and not wait for government.
S3.think: It's a window: she'd qualify, grow the drone business and by 2031 be the local person who knows both robots and power. She's unsure how long that lasts but it would be hers.
S3.do: Pays off the drone and saves about a hundred a month for a workshop and kit. Takes online robot maintenance courses, studying with AI on the drive, and invites Ben's family to make it a family business.
S3.feel: Uneasy but energetic, like getting ready for a big harvest.
S3.quote: Things change, you either own a bit of the new thing or you work for someone who does.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her plan ownership instead of scrambling for it. She'd watch the largest local farm's purchases as her signal. Her focus on local and family ownership marks her traditional, free-market outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone willing to work, and there's no excuse for a town not to come out of it stronger. Keep families together, train young people, and make sure local businesses own the machines, not just big companies. I'd say it at the town meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do well. Ten years is enough to build a real business, servicing farm robots and line robots, with Ben and maybe his brother. I'd be thirty-seven and my own boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd qualify and keep growing the drone work. By year three, I'd want a small workshop and a business loan to buy a couple of my own robots to rent out to farms. I'd use AI to help write the business plan, and I'd pay for it all myself, not with grants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a little impatient to get started. It feels like it plays to everything I'm good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything worry you in the ten-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the big companies sell robots straight to farmers with their own repair people and cut out locals like me. That would sting. So I'd want to get in early and be trusted before they show up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing on an ordinary day in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Driving out to a farm with a robot in the back of the truck, probably still in my old lineworker boots. Fixing a sensor, chatting with the farmer over coffee. Not so different from now, really, just different tools.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift for anyone willing to work, and a town should come out stronger by keeping families together, training young people and making sure local businesses own the machines. She'd say it at the town meeting.
S4.think: She thinks she'd do well, building a business servicing farm and line robots with Ben and maybe his brother. At thirty-seven she'd be her own boss.
S4.do: Qualifies and grows the drone work in the first year, aiming for a workshop and a business loan by year three to buy robots to rent to farms. Writes the business plan with AI and funds it herself rather than with grants.
S4.feel: Calm and impatient to start, since it plays to everything she's good at.
S4.quote: Driving out to a farm with a robot in the back of the truck, probably still in my old lineworker boots.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years turns AGI from a threat into her business plan. Her one fear is big companies selling directly to farmers and cutting out locals. She'd refuse grants, preferring to fund it herself, in line with her self-reliant outlook.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd see exactly what to do and have no money to do it with. What would help is small business loans for local people, so it's not only big companies that own the robots, and employers training their people properly. Not handouts, just a fair shot at owning a piece.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I want this. Part of me does, which feels strange to say as a lineworker. But I'd still miss being up a pole at sunset over the Flats.

headlineQuote: With two weeks of savings and a drone on credit, I can't buy a robot, I can barely buy the batteries.
portrait: Zoe Schmidt is a 27-year-old first-year lineworker on a farm-country crew, living with her partner Ben above his family's farm supply shop and running a small weekend drone business she bought on credit. She uses AI every day and believes, like her grandfather, that you're not free until you own something. She's calm through the plateau and steady change, seeing drones as her way up, and anxious in the two-year AGI case only because she'd have no money to grab the opportunity. With five or ten years she plans a family business servicing farm and line robots, funded by loans rather than grants. She admits an awkward tension between her free-market views and her fear of a few giant companies owning everything.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most because she'd see exactly what to do but have no money to do it.
whatWouldHelp: Small business loans for local people so that not only big companies own the robots, plus employers training their people properly: a fair shot at owning a piece, not handouts.
